You understand and write in a press style: headlines, reporting verbs (afirmar, declarar, asegurar, señalar), “según”, the journalistic passive and the conditional of rumour (habría, sería).
According to our correspondent, the ceremony lasted an hour.
The bride stated that it had been the happiest day of her life.
The fire reportedly started at three in the morning.
The bridge was opened yesterday by the mayor.
Thousands of people are expected to attend the concert.
To recognise the structure of a news story: titular (headline), entradilla (lead paragraph), cuerpo (body).
To use reporting verbs: afirmar, declarar, asegurar, señalar, explicar, reconocer, anunciar.
To use “según + person/source” and the conditional of rumour: habría muerto, sería el mayor.
To use the journalistic passive: fue inaugurado, han sido detenidos.
To use se espera que / se calcula que / se cree que.

Kyoto, the morning after the wedding. At breakfast in the guesthouse, Mihai is reading an article on his phone by Javier Ruiz, the Tokyo correspondent of a Spanish newspaper and a friend of Takeshi’s, who was invited to the wedding.
Ana, look at this! Javier has published an article about the wedding. It’s in the culture section of his paper.
Really? And what headline did he give it?
“A Shinto wedding in three languages brings Japan, Spain and Romania together in Kyoto.”
What a journalist! He’s turned a wedding into international news. Go on, read it to me.
“Kyoto. The ceremony, which was held last Saturday at the Shimogamo shrine, had guests from three countries. According to the bride, Yuki Sato, Spanish was the language that united them all.”
Look at how he writes: “was held”, “had”, “according to the bride”. It’s typical press style.
Listen to this bit: “One of the guests, a seventy-year-old Romanian grandmother, reportedly got through airport security with three jars of homemade preserve.”
(laughs) “Reportedly”! As if he weren’t sure. You told him last night, didn’t you?
Guilty. But look at the conditional: newspapers use it when the information isn’t confirmed. It’s to protect themselves.
And does it say anything about Takeshi’s grandmother?
Yes, at the end: “The groom’s grandmother, Haruko Tanaka, told this newspaper that meeting the Romanian family on the plane had been not chance but destiny.”
I have to show it to Elena. Even if she won’t understand it, she’ll want to keep it. And to my students too: it’s the best text I could take to class.
Newsreaders speak slowly, with clear pauses after each piece of information: «Kioto. [pause] La ceremonia, [pause] que fue celebrada el sábado…»
a-BREE-a, seh-REE-a: stress on -RÍ-. The conditional of rumour is said in a neutral tone, without emotion.
ko-rres-pon-SAL: a rolled “rr”, stress on the last syllable.
1. The structure of a news story
the essentials; verb in the present or no verb
Una boda en tres idiomas reúne a tres países
Más de cien invitados asistieron a la ceremonia
first paragraph: who, what, where, when
Kioto. La ceremonia, celebrada el sábado…

Headlines often use the PRESENT for past events (“El Gobierno aprueba la ley”), just like English headlines (“Government approves law”), and the INFINITIVE for the future (“El alcalde, a inaugurar el puente mañana” — rare, mostly in short headlines).
Journalists avoid repeating the verb “decir”. They use more precise verbs, usually in the indefinido, followed by reported speech (ch. 47):
The minister maintained that the situation was under control.
According to the police, there were no injuries.
When the information is NOT confirmed, the press uses the conditional (simple for the present, compound for the past). In English: “reportedly”, “allegedly”, “is said to”.
The fire reportedly started in the kitchen.
The president is said to be ill.
The thieves allegedly fled in a red car.
In everyday speech, this conditional sounds very “newspapery”. In conversation, say instead: «Parece que…», «Dicen que…».
4. The passive and impersonal press structures
The bridge was opened yesterday. (passive with ser, ch. 45)
A thousand people are expected to come. (+ subjunctive)
The damage is estimated at a million.
The culprit is believed to be a neighbour.
“Se espera que” takes the subjunctive (it’s a hope/expectation). “Se calcula que / se cree que” take the indicative (they’re information).
Unconfirmed information: “The thieves allegedly fled in a car.”
Los ladrones huyeron en un coche.
Los ladrones habrían huido en un coche.
Los ladrones huyan en un coche.
Which verb do you use when someone admits a mistake?
El Gobierno aprueba la nueva ley
El Gobierno ha aprobado ayer por la tarde la nueva ley que…
Yo creo que el Gobierno aprueba la ley

Una boda sintoísta en tres idiomas reúne a Japón, España y Rumanía en Kioto

Kyoto. More than eighty guests from three countries attended the wedding of Yuki Sato and Takeshi Mori last Saturday, held according to the Shinto rite at the Shimogamo shrine, one of the oldest in Japan.

The couple met at a Spanish club in Kyoto. As the bride explained, “Spanish was our first common language, even though we’re both Japanese”. The couple stated that they will continue to speak Spanish at home.
Among the guests was a Romanian family, led by the Spanish teacher Ana Popescu, who reportedly travelled for more than fourteen hours with her daughter of almost four.

During the banquet, speeches were read in Japanese, Spanish and Romanian. It is estimated that more than two hundred cups of sake were served. Sources close to the family pointed out that the party ended after midnight.
¿Qué frase usa el condicional de rumor?
que habría viajado más de catorce horas

The wedding day began cold and clear, with a sky so blue it looked painted. At the guesthouse, from seven in the morning, nobody sat still. Takeshi’s family had sent two elderly ladies to help them put on their kimonos, because, as they explained, it was impossible to do it alone.

They were right. Ana’s kimono had so many layers, ribbons and knots that it took almost an hour to dress her. It was dark blue silk, with white cranes embroidered along the bottom. When she finally looked in the mirror, she didn’t recognise herself.

Mihai, in a black men’s kimono and wide grey-striped trousers, looked like a slightly bewildered samurai. Elena refused to wear the full kimono, but agreed to a haori, a silk jacket that she wore over her best dress. And Rosa Elena had a little red kimono with cherry blossoms, and wouldn’t stop twirling to see how the sleeves moved.

The Shimogamo shrine stands in the middle of an ancient forest, Tadasu no Mori, which according to tradition has existed for more than two thousand years. To reach the entrance you have to walk along a long gravel path between enormous trees. Ana remembered what Mrs Tanaka had told them on the plane: the sound of footsteps on the gravel and the silence of the forest. It was exactly like that.

The guests were waiting in front of the shrine’s great red gate. All the members of the Kyoto Spanish club were there, and they came to hug Ana as if she were family. Javier Ruiz, the correspondent who was Takeshi’s friend, was there too, with a notebook in his pocket and a camera round his neck.
And then they saw her. Among the groom’s relatives, dressed in a very elegant black kimono, was an elderly lady with white hair in a bun.
Mrs Tanaka came over smiling and bowed to them. Takeshi, who was arriving at that moment, stood open-mouthed.

It turned out that Haruko Tanaka was Takeshi’s mother’s mother. She had been coming back from her son’s in Vienna, Takeshi’s uncle, precisely to attend the wedding. When she saw a European family with a little girl and heard the mother speak a little Japanese, she suspected who they might be. When she heard the word “Shimogamo”, she was sure.
“And why didn’t you tell us?” Ana asked, half laughing, half surprised.

“Because the best surprises are the ones you keep,” the old lady answered. “And because I wanted to see what you were really like, without you knowing who I was. Now I know my grandson has good friends.”

At eleven sharp the procession began. At the front walked two priests dressed in white and two young shrine maidens, miko, in bright red skirts. Behind them came the bride and groom, shaded by a large red umbrella held by an attendant. At the back, in silence, walked the families and the guests.

Yuki was wearing shiromuku, the all-white bridal kimono, and a large white hood that covered her hair and almost her whole face. Ana, walking a few steps behind, could only see her profile. However calm she seemed, Ana knew she was trembling: you could see it in her hands.

Takeshi, beside her, in a black kimono with his family crest, walked very straight and very seriously. But when they passed Rosa Elena, who was watching them, fascinated, from her father’s arms, he winked at her.

The ceremony in the shrine was short and intense. Nobody spoke. All you could hear were the priest’s ancient words, the sound of the flute and, now and then, the wind in the trees. Ana understood almost nothing, but there was no need.

At the most important moment, the couple drank sake from three small cups, one after the other, three sips from each. Mrs Tanaka, sitting next to Ana, whispered the explanation: it was called san-san-kudo, “three times three, nine”, and it symbolised the union of the two families.
Then Takeshi read his vows in Japanese. And after that, to everyone’s surprise, Yuki took a little piece of paper out of the sleeve of her kimono and read hers in Spanish.
“Takeshi: I promise that, however hard life gets, I will always be waiting for you with a hot dinner. Well, almost always.”

The members of the Spanish club burst into a roar of laughter that echoed through the whole shrine. The Japanese relatives, who hadn’t understood a thing, looked at each other in bewilderment. The priest frowned. And Takeshi, as red as the umbrella, tried not to laugh, without success.

The banquet was held in the afternoon at a traditional restaurant on the banks of the Kamo river. There were low tables, cushions on the floor and dishes so beautiful it seemed a shame to eat them. Javier Ruiz was taking notes in his notebook non-stop.

Then came the moment for presents. Elena stood up, in her silk haori, and gave the couple the hand-embroidered tablecloth and the three jars of zacuscă. Ana translated her words into Spanish, and Takeshi translated them into Japanese for his family:
“Where I come from, we say a house isn’t a home until there’s a table with a tablecloth and food made with love. I can’t speak Japanese or Spanish. But I can cook. That’s what I know how to say.”

There was silence. Then Takeshi’s mother stood up, went over to Elena and bowed so deeply she almost touched the floor. Elena, not knowing what to do, hugged her. The two mothers stayed like that for a long time.

Ana handed over Mrs Tanaka’s senbazuru and told the story of the plane. When she had finished, Haruko Tanaka stood up and announced, in a firm voice, that she hadn’t made those cranes during the flight: she had started folding them a year earlier, when Takeshi told her he was getting married. She had made nine hundred and ninety-nine. The last one, the thousandth, she had made on the plane, in front of Rosa Elena.
“It’s the red crane,” she said, pointing at the little girl, who was asleep on a cushion, still holding the crane. “She has the thousandth. So now this little girl is part of the family too.”
Ana couldn’t hold back her tears. Neither could Yuki. And Javier Ruiz, the journalist, stopped writing for the first time all day.

The party went on until after midnight. There were speeches in three languages, karaoke songs in Japanese, a disastrous attempt by Mihai to sing a Spanish song and a whole hour in which Elena taught the Mori family to dance a hora, with more enthusiasm than technique.
At the end of the night, Yuki and Ana stepped out for a moment onto the riverbank. The water flowed dark and quiet under the lantern lights.
“Do you remember the first time we spoke?” asked Yuki. “I couldn’t even say ‘me llamo’.”
“And now you’ve made a whole shrine laugh in Spanish,” Ana answered. “The hot-dinner thing will be in the paper, you’ll see.”
She was right. The next day, Javier Ruiz’s article began with that very sentence.

And under the headline, in small letters, Javier had added a note that made Ana smile all the way home: “According to sources close to the family, crane number one thousand is already on its way to Bucharest, in the hand of a little Romanian girl who, from now on, reportedly has grandparents on two continents”.
